item.title: AWS Continuum Experiment: Findings, Fixes, and Cost
item.description:
I connected AWS Continuum to my mem9 deployment to see whether an AI security service could move beyond reporting vulnerabilities and help deliver verified fixes. It did produce useful remediation work. It also exposed two costs I had underestimated: the engineering needed to admit generated patches safely, and the inference cost of a full repository scan.

The experiment covered a codebase of roughly 233,000 lines across 704 files. My investigation put one full scan at roughly $250–370 in inference charges, based on approximate scan-window attribution. That is an observation from this workload, not a fixed price per scan or a quote for another repository.

item.title: Self-Hosted GitHub Runners on AWS Spot for AI Dev Teams
item.description:
Autonomous AI dev teams move the bottleneck. When a dispatcher fans out work to dev and review agents every 5 minutes, the constraint is no longer human attention — it is the CI/CD pipeline that gates every PR. Each agent push triggers builds, tests, E2E verification, and bot reviews. With even a small team of agents iterating in parallel, GitHub Actions minutes become the dominant operational cost.

Hosted runners are convenient, but they are billed per-minute and capped at 2 cores on the standard tier. For a team of agents that pushes dozens of times an hour and runs container builds + Playwright suites, the math stops working. The lever is self-hosted runners on AWS spot EC2 — bigger instances, multi-architecture, scaling to zero when idle.
